knowledge_sections.title: Core concepts
knowledge_sections.summary: Quantitative trading means turning an idea into explicit rules, testable data assumptions and repeatable review steps.
beginner_actions: Write down the rule in plain language before coding it.
Keep the first strategy narrow enough that you can explain every input.
avoid_for_now: Do not start from dozens of indicators and ad-hoc parameter tuning.
Do not treat a narrative or a chatbot summary as a trade signal by itself.
examples: A simple example is: only observe symbols with stable liquidity, positive trend and a clear invalidation level.
warnings: If you cannot describe why a rule should stop working, you do not understand the strategy boundary yet.

knowledge_sections.title: Research workflow
knowledge_sections.summary: A safer workflow is hypothesis -> data check -> backtest -> simulation -> review, not idea -> live trade.
beginner_actions: Record sample period, fee/slippage assumptions and what counts as a failure.
Split validation into at least development and out-of-sample review.
avoid_for_now: Do not trust a single backtest run without checking another market regime.
examples: A rule that looks great only in one strong trend year should stay in research or simulation.
warnings: Missing data-quality checks can create false confidence through look-ahead bias or survivor bias.

terms.definition: A period not used to design the rule.
terms.example: It is the closest thing to a fair exam for the strategy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Good in-sample performance does not imply good out-of-sample performance.

terms.definition: The difference between expected execution price and actual execution price.

knowledge_sections.title: Risk control
knowledge_sections.summary: For beginners, position sizing, diversification and pause rules are often more important than finding one more indicator.
beginner_actions: Define single-position and portfolio exposure limits before the first paper trade.
Limit watchlist size so you can review every name properly.
avoid_for_now: Do not increase risk because one recent trade worked well.
Do not concentrate several highly related names into one theme bet without noticing it.
examples: Owning several AI-chip names can look diversified by ticker count but still be one theme exposure.
warnings: If drawdown, execution anomaly or data anomaly is triggered, the next step should usually be review, not more trading.

terms.definition: How much capital one idea is allowed to use.

terms.definition: How much money a strategy can realistically handle.
terms.example: A minute-level strategy on illiquid names has lower capacity than a daily large-cap strategy.
terms.common_misunderstanding: Capacity is not only about account size; it is also about liquidity.

rendered_documents.body:
### Beginner Quant Research

- Generated at: 2026-05-11T00:21:09.417827+08:00
- Version: v1
- Audience: beginner quant trader

### What this note is trying to do
- Explain the key ideas in plain language.
- Tell you what to do first, what to avoid for now, and what must be verified before upgrading stages.
- Keep research, execution advice and risk prompts separate.

### Learning order
- Understand core concepts and risk language before touching execution settings.
- Learn the research workflow: hypothesis -> data check -> backtest -> simulation -> review.
- Study a small candidate set and explain why each name is on the list.
- Write a risk budget and pause rules before any simulation session.

### Practice order
- Run the read-only health check first.
- Review research findings and evidence levels.
- Check the watchlist or candidate observations and keep only a few names.
- Review one backtest or validation summary before any simulation idea.
- Move to simulation only after risk budget and readiness checklist are both clear.

### Current assumptions
- evidence_scope: public_and_verifiable_only — Prefer public sources that can be revisited later.
- default_frequency: low_frequency_first — Beginners should optimise for explainability and reviewability.
- llm_role: research_assistant_only — LLM output should not bypass risk controls or directly place trades.

### Knowledge sections
#### Core concepts
- Summary: Quantitative trading means turning an idea into explicit rules, testable data assumptions and repeatable review steps.
- What you can do now:
  - Write down the rule in plain language before coding it.
  - Keep the first strategy narrow enough that you can explain every input.
- What to avoid for now:
  - Do not start from dozens of indicators and ad-hoc parameter tuning.
  - Do not treat a narrative or a chatbot summary as a trade signal by itself.
- Examples:
  - A simple example is: only observe symbols with stable liquidity, positive trend and a clear invalidation level.
- Warnings:
  - If you cannot describe why a rule should stop working, you do not understand the strategy boundary yet.
- Key terms:
  - factor: A measurable input that may explain return differences.
    - Example: Momentum and quality are common factors.
    - Common misunderstanding: A factor is not a guaranteed edge forever.
  - max drawdown: The largest peak-to-trough loss during a period.
    - Example: A strategy up 20% but down 15% along the way still has a painful drawdown.
    - Common misunderstanding: High return with unmanageable drawdown is not beginner friendly.
  - turnover: How frequently the portfolio changes.
    - Example: Higher turnover usually means more cost and more execution sensitivity.
    - Common misunderstanding: High turnover is not automatically better.
#### Research workflow
- Summary: A safer workflow is hypothesis -> data check -> backtest -> simulation -> review, not idea -> live trade.
- What you can do now:
  - Record sample period, fee/slippage assumptions and what counts as a failure.
  - Split validation into at least development and out-of-sample review.
- What to avoid for now:
  - Do not trust a single backtest run without checking another market regime.
- Examples:
  - A rule that looks great only in one strong trend year should stay in research or simulation.
- Warnings:
  - Missing data-quality checks can create false confidence through look-ahead bias or survivor bias.
- Key terms:
  - out-of-sample: A period not used to design the rule.
    - Example: It is the closest thing to a fair exam for the strategy.
    - Common misunderstanding: Good in-sample performance does not imply good out-of-sample performance.
  - slippage: The difference between expected execution price and actual execution price.
    - Example: Fast intraday strategies are much more sensitive to slippage.
    - Common misunderstanding: Ignoring slippage can make a fragile strategy look good.
#### Risk control
- Summary: For beginners, position sizing, diversification and pause rules are often more important than finding one more indicator.
- What you can do now:
  - Define single-position and portfolio exposure limits before the first paper trade.
  - Limit watchlist size so you can review every name properly.
- What to avoid for now:
  - Do not increase risk because one recent trade worked well.
  - Do not concentrate several highly related names into one theme bet without noticing it.
- Examples:
  - Owning several AI-chip names can look diversified by ticker count but still be one theme exposure.
- Warnings:
  - If drawdown, execution anomaly or data anomaly is triggered, the next step should usually be review, not more trading.
- Key terms:
  - position sizing: How much capital one idea is allowed to use.
    - Example: A good idea can still hurt if the size is too large.
    - Common misunderstanding: Entry direction and position size are separate decisions.
  - capacity: How much money a strategy can realistically handle.
    - Example: A minute-level strategy on illiquid names has lower capacity than a daily large-cap strategy.
    - Common misunderstanding: Capacity is not only about account size; it is also about liquidity.
#### Performance evaluation
- Summary: Headline return is incomplete; you need return, drawdown, risk-adjusted return, turnover, sample size and stability together.
- What you can do now:
  - Review both return and the path taken to achieve it.
  - Keep a small scorecard for every strategy version and compare changes carefully.
- What to avoid for now:
  - Do not upgrade a strategy just because one parameter set has the highest profit.
- Examples:
  - A slightly lower return with much smaller drawdown and lower turnover may be the better beginner choice.
- Warnings:
  - If a strategy only wins after aggressive tuning, it may be overfit rather than robust.
- Key terms:
  - Sharpe ratio: A rough measure of return per unit of volatility.
    - Example: Higher is usually better, but only when sample quality is acceptable.
    - Common misunderstanding: Sharpe alone does not capture tail risk or execution friction.
  - stability: Whether results stay reasonable across periods, assets or parameter ranges.
    - Example: A robust rule should not collapse after a small parameter change.
    - Common misunderstanding: The best single backtest number is not the same as stability.

### Research conclusions
- [high] Beginners should prioritise evidence-backed, low-frequency and reviewable workflows over minute-level automation.
- [high] Out-of-sample checks, transaction costs and data-quality notes are mandatory before moving beyond research or backtest summaries.
- [mid] LLM tools are useful for evidence summarisation and candidate explanation, but they should remain research helpers rather than execution authorities.
- [mid] A written risk budget and stop conditions should exist before the first simulation session, not after the first drawdown.

### Common pitfalls
- Confusing a good story with a tested rule.
- Looking only at return and ignoring drawdown, turnover and sample quality.
- Adding too many correlated names and calling it diversification.
- Letting an LLM summary replace manual review of evidence and risk controls.
- Do not move to live trading until reconciliation, logging and approval controls are in place.
- If a result depends on minute-level execution, add stricter cost and latency assumptions.

### Minimum viable start
- One market, a small watchlist and a low-frequency review habit.
- A written risk budget with single-position, total-exposure and pause rules.
- At least one backtest or validation note with data-quality and cost assumptions recorded.
- A simulation observation period before any live intent.

### Readiness checkpoints
- No readiness checklist has been attached yet.

### What changed from the previous plan
- No previous plan comparison was available for this run.

### Personalization summary
- No explicit personalization summary was recorded for this artifact.

### Update scope
- No scoped profile update information was recorded.

### Next actions
- Start from research, explanation and backtest review before any simulation step.
- Use LLM results as an evidence summary, not as a direct execution instruction.
- Keep a small watchlist and define pause conditions before the first paper trade.

### Local system boundaries
- Execution-related stages still require explicit confirmation and should default to plan-only mode.
- The following local entries require confirmation before execution: scripts/classic_multifactor/run_daily_rebalance.py, scripts/classic_multifactor/run_intraday_loop.py, scripts/classic_multifactor/run_vnpy_cta_backtest.py, scripts/quant_workflow/run_quant_workflow.py, scripts/run_hk_futu_sim_session.py
